newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Economic gloom replaces Bulgarian euphoria.
newsitem.headline: Economic gloom replaces Bulgarian euphoria.

text.p: Bulgarians awoke on Saturday to the grim reality of hyper-inflation as the euphoria of month-long street protests wore off.

Many petrol stations were without fuel, state pharmacies were closed awaiting introduction of new prices on Monday, and newspapers speculated about how long bakers would be able to maintain the price of bread.
With monthly inflation put at 50 percent for January alone, on Thursday the cabinet doubled state salaries and the minimum monthly wage is now 11,000 levs, or about $3.60.
Markets were full of shoppers enjoying bright winter sunshine, but most were staring in disbelief at the prices rather than buying.

A loaf of bread currently costs about 250 levs with the help of government subsidies, but Standart daily forecast it could cost 1,300 levs in two weeks and reported pensioners besieging post offices to collect a one-off pension supplement worth just $2.
"Now a well-paid pensioner can afford to buy 10 loaves of bread," the paper said, comparing the minimum pension of 2,808 levs with the 3,000 lev cost of a kilo (two lbs) of meat.

Bulgaria's main refinery has no cash to buy imported crude oil, and Sofia transport is threatened with closure from Tuesday because of lack of diesel. Electricity prices will rise by 35 percent from February 15.
With an influenza epidemic sweeping the country, the Socialist daily Douma calculated medicines for a child could cost 15,000 levs.

After 30 days of mass anti-government protests fuelled by the economic hardship, President Petar Stoyanov on Tuesday brokered a deal under which the governing Socialists agreed to give up attempts to form a new cabinet.
Stoyanov must appoint a caretaker cabinet, expected to be led by Sofia's respected mayor, Stefan Sofianski. Elections are due by April 20.
The tiny rump Bulgarian Communist Party proposed shops should be looted and their stocks distributed among the people.
Communist Party leader Vladimir Spassov said salvation committees should be set up around the country to remove shopkeepers and to distribute food to the starving according to lists.

Pari financial daily warned pay rises won by strikers would only fuel hyper-inflation. "This was the longest and the biggest strike in Bulgarian trade union history but one result of that strike was promises of huge salaries and the printing of money began," the paper said.

Last year, the International Monetary Fund proposed a tough fixed exchange rate regime, strictly matching levs in circulation to central bank reserves, which would restore confidence and halt the collapse of the lev.

The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) papered over the cracks between its different factions on Friday, approving the decision to give up its mandate and saying deputies would attend parliament next week.

"The BSP assesses the early parliamentary elections as a primary political task and major factor for the party's consolidation and mobilisation, protecting the Leftist idea from Rightist extremism and revenge-seeking," a statement said.

The opposition Union of Democratic Forces has asked for an extraordinary session of parliament for Tuesday to discuss changes to the electoral law and the income tax law, and a bill giving a mandate to the caretaker cabinet to borrow funds for grain imports and negotiate with the IMF.
Four prominent Socialist deputies and the mayor of the town of Dobrich left the Socialist party, saying they would join the new Euroleft movement of liberal Marxist Alexander Tomov.
Nikolai Kamov, Elena Poptodorova, Filip Bokov and Ivailo Kalfin were all member's of the party's reformist wing and critics of outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov.
